Clinical Reference

Pulmonary Embolism

On this page
A thrombus — usually broken off a leg or pelvic DVT — lodges in the pulmonary arteries, obstructing flow, straining the right ventricle, and (when large enough) collapsing cardiac output into obstructive shock.
3rd most common acute cardiovascular syndrome Risk = hemodynamics + RV strain + troponin High-risk 30-day mortality >15% Anchor: anticoagulation ± reperfusion
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

PE is the lung end of one disease: venous thromboembolism (VTE). A clot forms in a deep vein — usually the proximal leg or pelvis — under Virchow's triad (venous stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability). A fragment breaks loose, rides the venous return through the right heart, and wedges in the pulmonary arteries.

Two problems follow. First, a gas-exchange problem: obstructed segments are ventilated but not perfused, creating dead space and V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia and, from reflex tachypnea, hypocapnia. Second — and what actually kills — a hemodynamic problem: mechanical obstruction plus hypoxic vasoconstriction and released mediators (thromboxane A₂, serotonin) drive up pulmonary vascular resistance. The thin-walled right ventricle was never built to generate a mean PA pressure much above ~40 mmHg acutely, so it dilates and fails. As the RV balloons, the interventricular septum bows leftward (the echo "D-sign"), throttling LV filling. Cardiac output falls, coronary perfusion of the stretched RV wall drops, RV ischemia worsens the failure — the "RV death spiral" of obstructive shock.

Think of the pulmonary circulation as a highway on-ramp. A stalled truck (the embolus) blocks lanes; traffic (blood) backs up behind it (the RV), while the road ahead (the LV) runs empty. Anticoagulants stop more trucks from piling on and let the tow crew (endogenous fibrinolysis) work; thrombolytics are the tow crew on overdrive that actively dissolves the truck; embolectomy is a crane that hauls it out; pressors keep the backed-up engine (RV) running until the lane clears.

Pathophysiologic cascade — DVT → embolization → ↑PVR → RV failure → obstructive shock, with the step each therapy class interrupts.
Embolus lodged at the pulmonary artery, arising from a lower-extremity DVT.
Image: https://www.scientificanimations.com, 3D Medical Animation still shot Pulmonary Embolism.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Gross pathology — a thromboembolus straddling a pulmonary artery at autopsy.
Image: Dr. Rocke Robertson, AC08-7 Pulmonary embolus.JPG (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Anticoagulation (heparin, LMWH, fondaparinux, DOACs, warfarin) does not dissolve existing clot — it halts propagation and new thrombus so the body's own plasmin can remodel the embolus; it is the anchor for every PE. Thrombolysis (alteplase, tenecteplase) activates plasminogen to actively lyse clot — reserved for the failing RV. Embolectomy (catheter or surgical) physically debulks clot. Norepinephrine + dobutamine and cautious fluids support the RV until the obstruction resolves.
🔎

Presentation — symptoms & signs (frequency + why)

PE is a great mimic: no symptom is sensitive or specific. In PIOPED II, one of dyspnea, tachypnea, or pleuritic chest pain was present in 92% of confirmed PE — but each alone is unreliable. Frequencies below are from PIOPED I/II and the Stein 800-case registry.

Symptom / sign≈ FrequencyWhy it happens
Dyspnea (rest or exertion)~73–85%V/Q mismatch + dead space → hypoxemia; RV failure raises pulmonary pressures and stimulates J-receptors
Tachypnea (RR ≥20) — most common sign~54–70%Hypoxemia + reflex stimulation of pulmonary stretch/irritant receptors drive minute ventilation
Pleuritic chest pain~44–66%Distal emboli infarct lung abutting the pleura → localized pleural inflammation
Signs of DVT (unilateral leg swelling/pain)~40–47%The embolic source itself — residual proximal leg/pelvic clot obstructing venous return
Cough~34–43%Bronchial irritation and atelectasis around infarcted/underperfused lung
Tachycardia (HR >100)~24–30%Sympathetic response to hypoxemia and falling stroke volume; compensatory to preserve output
Orthopnea~28%Positional worsening of V/Q matching and venous return in a failing RV
Accentuated P2 / loud S2~15–23%Acute pulmonary hypertension increases the force of pulmonic valve closure
Hemoptysis~10–13%Pulmonary infarction with alveolar hemorrhage into airways (bronchial-artery collateral bleeding)
Syncope / presyncope~10–14%Transient drop in cardiac output from a large central clot; marks higher-risk PE
Low-grade fever (<38.5°C)~14%Inflammatory response to pulmonary infarction / thrombus
Hypotension / shock~5–8%Obstructive shock — RV failure and septal bowing collapse LV output; defines high-risk PE
Unexplained persistent tachycardia or isolated dyspnea with a clear chest X-ray is PE until proven otherwise — especially post-op, post-partum, or with cancer. Syncope in a dyspneic patient shifts you toward a large, central, higher-risk PE.
🗂️

Classification & severity (ESC 2019)

ESC 2019 replaced "massive / submassive / low-risk" with an early-mortality risk scheme built first on hemodynamic instability, then on clinical severity (PESI), RV dysfunction, and troponin. The old AHA terms are still spoken on rounds, so both are shown.

ESC risk classHemodynamic instabilityPESI III–V / sPESI ≥1RV dysfunction (echo/CT)Troponin ↑~30-day mortality
HighYes(usually)YesYes>15%
Intermediate-highNoYesBoth presentBoth present~5–15%
Intermediate-lowNoYesOne or neither positiveOne or neither positive~3–5%
LowNoNo (PESI I–II / sPESI 0)None (optional)None<1–2%
Hemodynamic instability = high-risk PE if ANY of: (1) cardiac arrest needing CPR; (2) obstructive shock — SBP <90 mmHg or vasopressors needed to keep SBP ≥90 despite filling, PLUS end-organ hypoperfusion (altered mentation, cold clammy skin, oliguria, lactate ↑); (3) persistent hypotension — SBP <90 or a drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min not from arrhythmia, hypovolemia, or sepsis. (ESC 2019, Table 4)
DescriptorMeaningNote
Saddle PEThrombus straddling the main PA bifurcationAnatomic term ≠ high-risk — many are stable; treat by hemodynamics/RV strain, not location
Subsegmental PE (SSPE)Isolated subsegmental filling defect, no proximal clot/DVTCHEST 2021: clinical surveillance over anticoagulation if low recurrence risk + negative proximal leg US
Provoked vs unprovokedPresence/absence of a transient major risk factorDrives duration of anticoagulation (see Clinic)
CTEPHChronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertensionOrganized thrombus + PH persisting >3 mo despite therapeutic anticoagulation; ~3% after acute PE

Assess

When to suspect & risk factors

🔍

Who walks in with PE — and what raises risk

Suspect PE in any patient with new dyspnea, pleuritic pain, unexplained tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, or signs of DVT. The pretest probability drives everything downstream — a low-probability patient can be safely ruled out with a rule (PERC) or a D-dimer, while a high-probability patient goes straight to imaging.

Strength (ESC 2019)Provoking factors
Strong (OR >10)Lower-limb fracture; hip/knee replacement; major trauma; spinal cord injury; MI or hospitalization for HF/AF within 3 months; prior VTE
Moderate (OR 2–9)Active cancer (highest with metastasis); central lines; chemotherapy; estrogen (OCP/HRT), IVF, postpartum; autoimmune/IBD; infection; CHF/respiratory failure; superficial vein thrombosis; thrombophilia
Weak (OR <2)Bed rest >3 days; prolonged travel/immobility; advancing age; obesity; pregnancy; laparoscopic surgery; diabetes; hypertension; varicose veins
Inherited/acquired thrombophilias: Factor V Leiden (most common, ~3–8× if heterozygous), prothrombin G20210A (~2–3×), protein C/S and antithrombin deficiency (rarer, higher relative risk), and antiphospholipid syndrome (acquired — the one that changes drug choice: use warfarin, avoid DOACs).

Treat

Anticoagulation — agents, doses & duration

💊

Stepwise choice — first-line → special situations

Every agent below interrupts the same step — clot propagation — so endogenous fibrinolysis can remodel the embolus. DOACs and heparins hit factor Xa/thrombin directly; warfarin depletes vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X.
1
First-line: a DOAC (single-drug, no lead-in for apixaban/rivaroxaban)
Preferred over warfarin in most patients (ESC 2019 / ASH 2020 / CHEST 2021)
▾
DrugStart / loadingMaintenance → extendedWhy it worksCautions / avoid
Apixaban10 mg BID × 7 days5 mg BID; 2.5 mg BID for extended therapy after ≥6 moDirect factor Xa inhibitorLeast GI bleeding; preferred in luminal-GI cancer. Avoid in APS, pregnancy
Rivaroxaban15 mg BID × 21 days (with food)20 mg once daily; 10 mg daily extendedDirect factor Xa inhibitorTake with food for absorption; ↑GI bleed in GI/GU cancer
EdoxabanParenteral lead-in ≥5 days first60 mg once daily (30 mg if ≤60 kg, CrCl 30–50, or P-gp inhibitor)Direct factor Xa inhibitorNeeds heparin/LMWH bridge; ↑GI bleed in cancer
DabigatranParenteral lead-in ≥5 days first150 mg BIDDirect thrombin (IIa) inhibitorNeeds lead-in; dyspepsia; avoid CrCl <30
If the home DOAC is unknown and the patient is stable: start therapeutic LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h) while you clarify the regimen — never guess a DOAC "restart phase."

Antiphospholipid syndrome (especially triple-positive) is the key DOAC exception — use warfarin; DOACs had higher arterial thrombosis in trials.

Duration — how long to anticoagulate

ScenarioDurationBasis
Provoked by a major transient factor (e.g. surgery)3 months, then stopLow recurrence once the trigger resolves
Minor transient factor or first unprovoked PE≥3 months; consider extendedWeigh recurrence vs bleeding (assess annually)
Recurrent unprovoked VTE, APS, or active cancerIndefinite / extendedHigh recurrence risk
Extended therapy, reduced dose (after ≥6 mo)Apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg dailyAMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN CHOICE — recurrence ↓ without excess major bleeding
When anticoagulation is stopped in unprovoked VTE and prevention is still wanted, aspirin is better than nothing but inferior to a DOAC — ASH 2020 favors continuing low-dose anticoagulation over aspirin in eligible patients.
Monitor

Follow-up & monitoring

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • DOACs: no routine level monitoring. Check renal + hepatic function at baseline and at least annually (more often if CrCl 30–60 or age >75); reassess weight and interacting drugs.
  • Warfarin: INR every few days until stable, then space to every 4 weeks; target 2.0–3.0.
  • LMWH: anti-Xa only in pregnancy, obesity, or renal impairment; monitor platelets for HIT (days 4–14).
  • Bleeding + recurrence review at each visit; reassess whether to continue extended therapy annually.
  • 3–6 month follow-up: if persistent dyspnea or exercise limitation, screen for CTEPH — start with a V/Q scan (high sensitivity); confirm with right-heart catheterization.
Prevent

Prevention & USPSTF

🛡️

Reducing the next clot

GradeRecommendationRelevance to PE
BDo not routinely screen the general population for inherited thrombophilia; testing rarely changes managementReserve testing for select cases; it seldom alters duration decisions
BCounsel on VTE risk with combined hormonal contraception / HRT, especially with other risk factorsEstrogen is a modifiable moderate risk factor

Practical prevention: mechanical + pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis for hospitalized and post-operative patients (the single biggest lever); early mobilization; ambulation and hydration on long-haul travel; graduated compression for high-risk travelers; address reversible provokers (estrogen, immobility). No general-population PE screening exists — prevention is prophylaxis in at-risk settings.

Interactions

Comorbidity interactions

🔗

How comorbidities change PE management

ComorbidityEffect on courseEffect on management
Active cancerHigher recurrence + higher bleeding; hypercoagulableDOAC (apixaban/edoxaban/rivaroxaban) or LMWH; apixaban/LMWH preferred in luminal GI/GU cancer; treat indefinitely while cancer active
Renal impairment (CrCl <30)Drug accumulation → bleedingPrefer UFH; avoid fondaparinux + standard LMWH; apixaban has least renal clearance among DOACs
PregnancyHypercoagulable; fetal drug exposureLMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg BID); avoid DOACs and warfarin; V/Q or CTPA both acceptable for diagnosis
Antiphospholipid syndromeHigh arterial + venous recurrenceWarfarin (INR 2–3); avoid DOACs (higher event rates in trials)
Severe liver disease / coagulopathyBaseline bleeding + unreliable INRAvoid DOACs (Child-Pugh B/C for rivaroxaban); individualize; warfarin INR unreliable
ObesityDosing uncertainty at extremesDOACs reasonable at most weights; consider anti-Xa monitoring for LMWH at weight extremes
Prior GI bleed / thrombocytopenia↑ bleeding riskFavor apixaban; correct platelets; avoid concurrent antiplatelets/NSAIDs
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: DOACs in antiphospholipid syndrome, pregnancy, mechanical heart valves, severe renal (CrCl <15–30) or severe liver disease; NSAIDs and concurrent antiplatelets (additive bleeding — stop if not essential); strong CYP3A4/P-gp inducers or inhibitors (rifampin, azoles, HIV protease inhibitors) that shift DOAC levels; fondaparinux + LMWH when CrCl <30. Never combine an anticoagulant with a thrombolytic unless deliberately reperfusing.
Escalate

When to send to the ED / admit

🚑

Red flags — don't manage in clinic

Send to the ED immediately for: SBP <90 mmHg or hemodynamic instability; SpO₂ <90% or new supplemental-O₂ requirement; syncope; RV dysfunction or positive troponin; sPESI ≥1 / PESI class III–V; suspected high-risk PE; active bleeding or contraindication to outpatient anticoagulation; poor social support or inability to obtain/afford medication.
A confirmed low-risk PE (sPESI 0, HESTIA-negative, no RV strain, good support) can often be treated at home on a DOAC — but only after a deliberate risk-stratification, not by default.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management of stable PE
Admit

Who to admit & risk-stratify

📋

Admission criteria & severity index

Once PE is confirmed and the patient is normotensive, the ward question is: low-risk (home candidate) vs intermediate-risk (admit, monitor) vs intermediate-high (monitored bed / step-down). Stratify with PESI or sPESI plus troponin and RV assessment (echo or CT RV/LV ratio). HESTIA criteria decide home eligibility.

Admit (floor)Intermediate-low risk; sPESI ≥1 or PESI III–IV; hypoxemia needing O₂; comorbidity/social barrier to home care.Floor
Monitored / step-downIntermediate-high (RV dysfunction AND troponin +) — watch for decompensation; rescue lysis on standby.Telemetry
Consider homesPESI 0 AND HESTIA-negative AND no RV strain/troponin — DOAC, early follow-up.Discharge

Treat

Acute inpatient management

💊

Stepwise therapy on the floor

1
Anticoagulate — the anchor for every confirmed PE
DOAC single-drug, or LMWH/UFH; UFH if unstable or reperfusion possible
▾

Start immediately (see the Clinic drug tables for full doses). On the floor, most stable patients get a DOAC or therapeutic LMWH. Choose UFH infusion if there is any chance of needing thrombolysis/embolectomy, if CrCl <30, or if hemodynamics are borderline — its short half-life and reversibility make it the safest bridge.

Stopping propagation lets endogenous fibrinolysis shrink the clot over days to weeks; RV function usually recovers as afterload falls.
2
Support & watch — intermediate-risk
O₂, telemetry, cautious fluids, serial vitals/troponin
▾
  • O₂ to SpO₂ ≥90%; avoid over-diuresis (RV is preload-dependent).
  • Cautious fluids only if hypovolemic — a bolus >500 mL can over-distend the failing RV and worsen output.
  • Serial troponin + vitals; escalate at the first sign of tipping.
3
Rescue reperfusion — if they decompensate
Systemic lysis or catheter-directed therapy; call PERT/ICU
▾

An intermediate-high patient who becomes hypotensive or hypoxemic despite anticoagulation needs rescue reperfusion — systemic thrombolysis (or catheter-directed therapy / embolectomy) and ICU transfer. This is the PEITHO lesson: routine up-front lysis in intermediate-risk PE causes net harm (major/ intracranial bleeding), so reserve it for deterioration.

Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Hemodynamics: HR, BP, and any pressor need — the earliest signal of RV failure.
  • Oxygenation: SpO₂ and O₂ requirement — improving means the obstruction is remodeling.
  • Troponin trend in intermediate-risk (falling = reassuring).
  • Renal + hepatic function and platelets (HIT surveillance days 4–14 on heparin).
  • Bleeding assessment daily; hemoglobin if any concern.
  • Ambulation as tolerated — bed rest is not required once anticoagulated and stable.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of: SBP <90 mmHg or new vasopressor requirement; SpO₂ <90% despite high-flow O₂ or rising O₂ need; rising/persistently elevated lactate; worsening RV function or a rising troponin with clinical decline; syncope/arrhythmia; any candidate for thrombolysis, catheter therapy, or embolectomy; cardiac arrest.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: hemodynamically stable ≥24–48 h; SpO₂ ≥90% on room air (or a stable home-O₂ plan); on an established anticoagulation regimen the patient can obtain and afford; pain controlled on orals; no active bleeding; reliable follow-up arranged; education on adherence, bleeding precautions, and recurrence red flags.

Home

Stable, low/intermediate-low risk, independent, on a DOAC with follow-up.

Home health

Home + LMWH-teaching/INR-draw visits, or frail but stable.

SNF

Needs 24-h skilled nursing (e.g. new O₂, deconditioning), <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-critical-illness deconditioning able to tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day.

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs (e.g. vent weaning after massive PE).

Hospice / palliative

PE in advanced cancer with comfort-focused goals.
🫀 ICU — high-risk PE, reperfusion & RV support
Admit

ICU triggers — high-risk PE

🚨

When PE belongs in the unit

The ICU population is high-risk PE (hemodynamic instability) and intermediate-high patients who are decompensating. This is obstructive shock — the priorities are reperfusion and keeping the RV alive until the clot burden falls.

High-risk PE = reperfuse now. Confirm with bedside echo (RV dilation, D-sign, McConnell) if CTPA cannot be safely obtained, give UFH, and proceed to systemic thrombolysis (or catheter-directed / surgical embolectomy if lysis is contraindicated). Activate the PERT (Pulmonary Embolism Response Team) if available.
Saddle embolus at the main pulmonary artery bifurcation — a large central clot burden (not automatically high-risk; hemodynamics decide).
Image: James Heilman, MD, Pulmonary Embolism.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Apical 4-chamber echo — assess RV dilation (RV/LV >1), septal bowing (D-sign), TAPSE, and McConnell sign (apical sparing).
Image: Espinola-Zavaleta N, Soto ME, Castellanos LM, Játiva-Chávez S, Keirns C., LVNC3.jpg (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Arterial line for continuous BP (MAP target ≥65 mmHg); central access for vasopressors/inotropes.
  • Bedside echo serially to follow RV size/function and response to therapy.
  • Serial lactate (perfusion), ABG (oxygenation/ventilation), troponin, and coagulation profile — especially peri-thrombolysis.
  • Avoid aggressive volume: the failing RV is preload-sensitive. Give a small trial (≤500 mL) only if truly hypovolemic, and stop if CVP rises without a BP response.
The RV death spiral is a hypotension–ischemia loop: keep the MAP up (norepinephrine) to preserve RV coronary perfusion, and keep the RV off-loaded (reperfusion, avoid hypoxia/hypercapnia/acidosis which all raise PVR).
Reperfuse

Thrombolysis & clot removal

💥

Doses, regimens & contraindications

Thrombolytics convert plasminogen to plasmin, which actively digests the fibrin embolus — rapidly dropping PA pressure and off-loading the RV. This is the one setting where you accept a real bleeding risk to save the RV.
AgentStandard doseAccelerated / alternativeNotes
Alteplase (tPA)100 mg IV over 2 h (often 10 mg bolus + 90 mg over 2 h)Cardiac arrest / peri-arrest: 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min (max 50 mg). Reduced-dose "MOPETT": 50 mgFDA-approved for massive PE. Hold UFH during infusion; restart when aPTT ≤2× normal (no bolus)
Tenecteplase (TNK)Single weight-based IV bolus: <60 kg 30 mg · 60–69 kg 35 mg · 70–79 kg 40 mg · 80–89 kg 45 mg · ≥90 kg 50 mgUsed in PEITHOConvenient single bolus; not FDA-labeled for PE (off-label)
Streptokinase250,000 IU over 30 min, then 100,000 IU/h × 12–24 hAccelerated: 1.5 million IU over 2 hRarely used; allergic/hypotensive reactions
Urokinase4,400 IU/kg load, then 4,400 IU/kg/h × 12–24 h—Alternative where available
Absolute contraindications to lysis (ESC 2019): prior hemorrhagic stroke or stroke of unknown origin; ischemic stroke <6 mo; CNS neoplasm; major trauma/surgery/head injury <3 wk; active bleeding; bleeding diathesis. Relative: TIA <6 mo, oral anticoagulation, pregnancy/first postpartum week, non-compressible punctures, traumatic CPR, refractory HTN (SBP >180), advanced liver disease, infective endocarditis, active peptic ulcer.
1
Systemic thrombolysis
First-line reperfusion for high-risk PE without contraindication
▾

ASH 2020: for PE with hemodynamic compromise, thrombolysis + anticoagulation over anticoagulation alone. Fastest, most available. Give via a peripheral line while arranging further care.

2
Catheter-directed / mechanical therapy
When systemic lysis is contraindicated or fails, or as lower-bleeding alternative
▾
  • Ultrasound-assisted CDT (EKOS): low-dose tPA (~10 mg over 15 h, ULTIMA; ~24 mg over 12–24 h, SEATTLE II) improves RV/LV ratio with less bleeding than systemic dosing.
  • Large-bore mechanical thrombectomy (FlowTriever/Indigo): aspirates clot without a lytic — PEERLESS (2024) favored it over CDT on a composite driven by fewer deteriorations/ICU admissions.
3
Surgical embolectomy / ECMO
Failed or contraindicated lysis, or refractory shock
▾

Surgical embolectomy for high-risk PE with failed/contraindicated thrombolysis. VA-ECMO as a bridge in refractory obstructive shock or arrest, buying time for reperfusion or clot resolution.

IVC filter — reserved for anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation; does NOT replace anticoagulation once safe.
Image: https://www.scientificanimations.com, 3D Medical Animation Inferior Vena Filter.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Retrieved/pathologic thromboembolus — the target of embolectomy.
Image: Yale Rosen, Septic thromboembolus.jpg (CC BY-SA 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons
IVC filter only when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, or PE recurs despite therapeutic anticoagulation. ASH 2020 recommends against adding a filter to anticoagulation. Retrieve it once anticoagulation is safe.
Support

Hemodynamic support — pressors & inotropes

💉

Which drip for the failing RV

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeEffect in PEWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ > β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate)↑ SVR restores coronary perfusion of the RV; mild inotropyFirst-line pressor in PE shock
Dobutamineβ₁ > β₂2.5–10 mcg/kg/min↑ RV contractility & cardiac output; can lower PVRAdd for low output/RV dysfunction (with a pressor to offset vasodilation/hypotension)
Epinephrineβ₁, β₂, α₁ (dose-dependent)0.01–0.2 mcg/kg/minInotropy + vasoconstriction combinedRefractory shock; peri-arrest
VasopressinV₁ receptor0.01–0.04 units/min (fixed)↑ SVR without raising PVR (may spare pulmonary vasoconstriction)Adjunct when norepinephrine alone insufficient
Inhaled NO / inhaled epoprostenolSelective pulmonary vasodilatoriNO 5–40 ppm; inh. epoprostenol per protocolLowers PVR → off-loads RV, improves oxygenation without systemic hypotensionAdjunct in RV failure/refractory hypoxemia (bridge, not definitive)
The RV fails because afterload spiked and its own coronary supply dropped. Norepinephrine raises aortic root pressure to re-perfuse the RV wall; dobutamine squeezes the stunned RV harder; inhaled vasodilators selectively drop PVR (the afterload) without tanking systemic BP. Definitive off-loading is still reperfusion.
Airway

Respiratory support & intubation

🌬️

Oxygenate — and beware intubation

Support oxygenation first with high-flow nasal cannula or NIV. Intubation is dangerous in high-risk PE: sedation drops preload and SVR, positive-pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure and PVR, and the peri-intubation period can precipitate arrest in a preload-dependent, obstructed RV. If unavoidable, optimize hemodynamics first (pressors running), use a hemodynamically stable induction (e.g. etomamidate/ketamine), avoid large fluid boluses, and use lung-protective, low-tidal-volume settings with modest PEEP.

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: off vasopressors ≥12–24 h with a stable MAP; SpO₂ ≥90% on low-flow O₂ or room air; lactate normalized; troponin trending down and RV function improving on echo; no bleeding complication after any thrombolysis; on a stable therapeutic anticoagulation plan. Not yet if: still requiring any pressor, escalating O₂ needs, active bleeding, or persistent RV dysfunction with instability.

Then run the risk-stratification triage (below) in reverse — an ex-high-risk patient becomes an intermediate-risk floor patient, and eventually a low-risk outpatient on a DOAC with CTEPH follow-up at 3–6 months.

Risk-stratification & management triage (ESC 2019) — from confirmed PE to the correct level of care.
Pearls

Clinical pearls & pitfalls

💡

High-yield rules that change management

  1. Hemodynamics, not clot location, define risk. A "saddle PE" that is normotensive with a normal RV is intermediate-/low-risk; a segmental PE causing shock is high-risk. Treat the patient's physiology, not the CT caption.
  2. D-dimer rules out, never rules in. Its value is a high negative predictive value in low-probability patients. Use the age-adjusted cutoff (age×10 µg/L over 50) or YEARS to avoid unnecessary CTPA — but a positive D-dimer means nothing on its own.
  3. A normal ABG or A–a gradient does not exclude PE. Many PE patients have a normal room-air PaO₂; oxygenation is neither sensitive nor specific.
  4. Don't flood the failing RV. In RV strain, a fluid bolus >500 mL can over-distend the RV, worsen septal bowing, and drop cardiac output. If hypotensive with RV dysfunction, reach for norepinephrine early rather than more fluid.
  5. Reserve up-front thrombolysis for high-risk (unstable) PE. PEITHO showed routine lysis in intermediate-risk PE trades a small reduction in decompensation for a real excess of intracranial hemorrhage — give rescue lysis only if they deteriorate.
  6. UFH is the safest bridge when the situation is fluid. If thrombolysis, embolectomy, or a procedure is possible, or CrCl <30, choose the short-half-life, reversible UFH infusion over LMWH or a DOAC.
  7. Antiphospholipid syndrome is the DOAC exception. Use warfarin (INR 2–3); DOACs had higher thrombosis rates, especially in triple-positive patients.
  8. Pregnancy = LMWH. Avoid DOACs and warfarin; V/Q and CTPA are both acceptable for diagnosis (proximal leg ultrasound first if DVT signs).
  9. Intubation can kill a high-risk PE patient. Sedation + positive pressure drop preload and raise PVR in a preload-dependent, obstructed RV. Optimize hemodynamics first, or avoid intubation with HFNC/NIV.
  10. An IVC filter is not a treatment — it's a dam. Use only when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or PE recurs despite therapeutic anticoagulation, and retrieve it once anticoagulation is safe.
  11. Syncope in a dyspneic patient shifts you toward a large, central, higher-risk PE — lower your threshold for imaging and risk stratification.
  12. Follow up for CTEPH. ~3% of patients develop chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension; screen persistent dyspnea at 3–6 months with a V/Q scan (the sensitive test), and refer operable disease for pulmonary endarterectomy.
Cardiac arrest with suspected PE: continue high-quality CPR and give thrombolytics during the arrest if PE is the presumed cause — alteplase 50 mg IV bolus (or 0.6 mg/kg, max 50 mg), then continue CPR for at least 60–90 minutes before terminating, as return of circulation can be delayed. Consider VA-ECMO where available.
